source.title: Scaling Law Phenomena Across Regression Paradigms: Multiple and Kernel Approaches
source.authors: Yifang Chen; Xu-Yang Guo; Xiao-Yu Li; Ying-Yu Liang; Zhenmei Shi; Zhao Song

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to theoretical sketched multiple- and kernel-regression settings, rather than testing language models.
record.gate_note: The study reports theoretical bounds, not language-model experiments or a sweep over parameter count, training tokens, or compute. Its discussion of prior scaling-law papers is cited background, not a result of this study.
record.test_reason: This is a purely theoretical paper. It derives loss bounds for sketched multiple regression trained by one-pass SGD, with Gaussian features and an assumed power-law covariance spectrum. The power-law form follows from that assumed spectrum. No language model, image or video model, or other trained neural system is measured, and nothing is fitted or extrapolated. The result is a mathematical model of where scaling laws could come from. It does not test whether any version holds for real models, so it is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude they derived generalization-error bounds (approximation, bias and variance) and a scaling law for sketched multiple regression under Gaussianity, well-specification and power-law spectrum assumptions. They also say they extended this to kernel regression. The kernel case, however, is only a proof-sketch corollary with no explicit power-law rate.
record.recipe_differences: The paper gives theoretical bounds for sketched regression trained with one-pass SGD, rather than empirical language-model scaling sweeps and compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The results are conditional on the distributional assumptions, power-law covariance spectrum, sketching setup, and stepsize constraints; the paper does not compare alternative fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Under Gaussian features, a well-specified model, an isotropic parameter prior and eigenvalues λ_i=Θ(i^−a), sketched multiple regression trained by one-pass SGD has expected loss σ²+Θ(M^(1−a))+Θ((N_eff γ)^(−(a−1)/a)). Here M is sketch dimension (standing in for model size) and N_eff=n/log n.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theoretical models: in sketched linear or multiple regression with a power-law feature spectrum, loss is provably a sum of power laws in sketch dimension and effective sample size.

fits_no_version.finding: For sketched kernel regression, the paper gives only a corollary that the minimizer's error equals σ² plus the approximation error. No explicit rate is given, and the proof is by analogy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theoretical models: kernel regression with sketched features exhibits scaling-law behaviour.

record.problems: The evidence is theoretical and conditional on strong assumptions, with no empirical validation on language models. The kernel-regression corollary does not give an explicit power-law exponent or scaling curve.

untested.parts: No language-model pretraining loss and no sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No compute-optimal allocation analysis, even though the bound has both M and N_eff terms.
No image, video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer experiments. There are only theoretical bounds for sketched linear and kernel regression under assumed power-law spectra.
No comparison of fitting choices or published exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T3/'tests' with a V5 'supports' label is overturned. A theorem in a linear toy model whose power law is built in through the spectrum assumption does not test whether trained models in other modalities or regimes follow power laws. The theorem closely follows Lin et al. 2024 (linear regression) and Wu et al. 2022. The probability statements switch between m and M. Some proof steps (e.g. the lower bound in Lemma 5.3, maximized 'by setting k=0') are loosely argued. No empirical validation of any kind is given.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy measurements for language models, or sweeps over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from smaller runs to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens.
No comparison of architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

The study analyzes sketched regression under specified assumptions; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer. The kernel-regression result does not state an explicit power-law exponent.
No downstream-task performance or predictability from pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or evidence about disagreement between published exponents or curves bending away from power laws.

rows.subject: multiple regression (sketched predictor)
rows.operation_detail: Derives a theoretical scaling law for generalization loss under sketching and one-pass SGD.

conditions.value: Gaussian features; well-specified multiple regression; parameter prior E[W*W*⊤]=I; covariance eigenvalues λᵢ=Θ(i⁻ᵃ), a>1
n samples; N_eff=n/log(n); initial stepsize γ≤c for an a-dependent constant c>0
m-dimensional sketched predictor; probability over sketch matrix R

rows.uncertainty: Theorem states probability at least 1−e^(−Ω(M)) over sketch randomness; terms are given in Θ notation.
rows.note: The loss has power-law terms in sketch dimension and effective sample size times stepsize, under the theorem's assumptions; these are not parameter-count, token-count, or compute sweeps.
rows.check: This is a theorem about sketched linear multiple regression, not a measured loss of a language or other neural model. The terms are in sketch dimension M and N_eff·γ, under an assumed eigenvalue spectrum λ_i=Θ(i^−a). It is not a test of V5's 'other modalities and training regimes'. The text uses M and m interchangeably for sketch dimension.

conditions.value: Theorem 4.5 assumptions, including Gaussianity, a well-specified model, parameter prior, and power-law covariance spectrum

rows.uncertainty: Theorem states probability at least 1−e^(−Ω(M)) over sketch randomness for the stated bounds.
rows.note: The text gives this approximation-error scaling as a separate component of the generalization-loss analysis.
rows.check: This is a component bound, approximation error Θ(m^(1−a)), inside the same theorem as r1. It is a derived consequence of the assumed power-law spectrum, not an empirical scaling result. It largely duplicates r1.

rows.note: The corollary states a bound but gives no explicit power-law exponent or dependence on sketch dimension or sample size.
